paddy_blast_description: Your AI scan detected signs of Paddy Blast, a fungal disease that can spread quickly in humid weather and significantly reduce yield if untreated.
paddy_blast_overview_text: Paddy Blast is caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae. It produces diamond-shaped lesions on leaves and can affect stems and panicles, causing major yield loss if left untreated, especially in humid conditions.
paddy_blast_water_text:
• Avoid water stress - keep fields consistently flooded where possible
• Avoid excess nitrogen, which increases susceptibility
• Improve field drainage to reduce humidity around plants
• Space plants to improve airflow
paddy_blast_fertilizer_text:
• Reduce nitrogen application, especially late-season doses
• Apply balanced NPK fertilizer rather than nitrogen-heavy mixes
• Consider silicon-based fertilizer, which strengthens leaf cell walls against fungal entry
paddy_blast_chemical_text:
Apply a fungicide such as Tricyclazole or Isoprothiolane 40% EC.
Dosage: follow the product label (commonly around 1.5ml per liter of water).
Spray at first sign of lesions and repeat every 7-10 days if symptoms continue.
paddy_blast_prevention_text:
• Use blast-resistant rice varieties where available
• Avoid dense planting
• Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest
• Rotate crops where practical
brown_spot_description: Your AI scan detected signs of Brown Spot, a fungal disease often linked to nutrient-poor soil, particularly low potassium.
brown_spot_overview_text: Brown Spot is caused by the fungus Bipolaris oryzae. It appears as small brown oval lesions on leaves and grains, and is strongly associated with potassium-deficient or poorly managed soil.
brown_spot_water_text:
• Maintain consistent water levels - avoid letting fields dry out and re-flood repeatedly
• Ensure adequate drainage to prevent waterlogging
• Reduce leaf wetness duration where possible
brown_spot_fertilizer_text:
• Correct potassium deficiency - apply Muriate of Potash if soil tests show low K
• Apply balanced NPK fertilizer rather than nitrogen alone
• Improve overall soil fertility with organic matter or compost
brown_spot_chemical_text:
Apply a fungicide such as Mancozeb or Propiconazole.
Dosage: follow product label instructions.
Spray at early symptom onset and repeat every 10-14 days if the disease persists.
brown_spot_prevention_text:
• Use disease-resistant varieties where available
• Test soil before planting to catch nutrient deficiencies early
• Use certified, disease-free seed
• Avoid excessive plant density
bacterial_leaf_blight_description: Your AI scan detected signs of Bacterial Leaf Blight. Unlike the other diseases this app detects, this one is bacterial, not fungal - fungicides will not work against it.
bacterial_leaf_blight_overview_text: Bacterial Leaf Blight is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas oryzae. It produces yellowish, water-soaked lesions along leaf veins that expand and dry out, and spreads rapidly through irrigation water, especially after storms or flooding.
bacterial_leaf_blight_water_text:
• Avoid overhead irrigation and standing floodwater where possible - this disease spreads through water
• Improve field drainage
• Avoid working in fields when foliage is wet, which can spread the bacteria
• Drain and dry the field if an outbreak is detected
bacterial_leaf_blight_fertilizer_text:
• Reduce nitrogen fertilizer - excess nitrogen increases susceptibility
• Apply balanced NPK rather than nitrogen-heavy fertilizer
• Ensure adequate potassium, which improves resistance
bacterial_leaf_blight_chemical_text:
This is a BACTERIAL disease, not fungal - standard fungicides will not work.
Apply a copper-based bactericide (e.g. copper oxychloride) or a locally approved streptomycin-based product.
Consult local agricultural extension services for products approved in your area.
bacterial_leaf_blight_prevention_text:
• Use resistant rice varieties where available
• Use certified, pathogen-free seed
• Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization
• Improve field drainage and avoid water stagnation
• Disinfect farm tools between fields
healthy_leaf_description: Great news - your AI scan didn't detect any signs of disease. Your crop looks healthy. Keep monitoring regularly and maintain good field management practices.
paddy_blast_info_causative: Caused by the fungus Magnaporthe grisea (Pyricularia grisea).
paddy_blast_info_affected: Can infect the plant at any growth stage - leaves, nodes, panicles, or seeds. Depending on the part infected, it is called leaf blast, nodal blast, panicle blast, or neck blast.
paddy_blast_info_symptoms: Spindle-shaped leaf spots with brown or reddish/yellowish-brown margins, ashy centers, and pointed ends, typically 1.0-1.5cm long and 0.3-0.5cm wide. Infected nodes turn black and rot. Infection at the panicle base causes neck rot, making the panicle fall off. Severe infection produces partly filled grains known as "whiteheads".
paddy_blast_info_conditions: Favoured by low night temperatures (17-20°C), high humidity, excessive nitrogen fertilizer, foggy or dark conditions, and dense planting.
paddy_blast_info_chemical: If the disease spreads quickly, fungicides can be applied: Tebuconazole 250g/l EC (10ml per 16L water), Isoprothiolane 400g/l EC (20ml per 16L water), Carbendazim 50% WP/WG (11g or 11ml per 16L water), or Tricyclazole 75% WP (10g per 16L water) - all at 8-10 tanks per acre.
paddy_blast_info_management_season: Apply urea at the recommended dosage, or based on a leaf colour chart. Manage weeds in the field.
paddy_blast_info_management_next: Use resistant varieties (Bg 403, Bg 406, Bg 366, Bg 359, Bw 361, Bg 250). Use certified, disease-free seed paddy. Add burnt paddy husk (250kg per acre) during land preparation. Avoid adding disease-infected straw to the field.
paddy_blast_info_varieties: Known susceptible varieties: Bg 358, Bg 357, Bg 360, Bw 367, At 373, Bg 94/1.
brown_spot_info_causative: Caused by the fungus Cochliobolus miyabeanus (Bipolaris oryzae).
brown_spot_info_affected: Affects coleoptiles, leaves, leaf sheaths, immature florets, panicle branches, glumes, and grains. Spots appear from early growth but become more common as plants approach maturity. It is a seed-borne disease.
brown_spot_info_symptoms: Brown, circular to oval spots appear on the coleoptile, which can cause seedling blight and weak, sparse plant stands. Spots are smaller on young leaves and larger on older leaves, ranging from small dark brown or reddish-brown spots to larger oval spots with a dark brown margin and a light reddish-brown or gray center. Similar spots appear on the leaf sheath and hulls. Infected glumes show a general black discoloration, and infected immature florets can produce light-weight or chalky grains.
brown_spot_info_conditions: Favoured by temperatures of 16-36°C, high humidity (86-100%), nutrient-poor or problem soils (high salinity, iron toxicity), and drought stress.
brown_spot_info_management_season: Apply urea at the recommended dosage, or based on a leaf colour chart. Manage weeds in the field.
brown_spot_info_management_next: Apply organic fertilizer to improve soil quality. Use certified, disease-free seed paddy. Add burnt paddy husk (250kg per acre) to the soil during land preparation. Avoid adding disease-infected straw to the field. Treat seed paddy by dipping in hot water (53-54°C) for 10-12 minutes. Treat seeds with a seed-protectant fungicide. Rotate crops. Ensure proper land levelling.
bacterial_leaf_blight_info_causative: Caused by the Bacteria, Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae.
bacterial_leaf_blight_info_affected: On seedling stage wilting and yellowing of leaves, or wilting of seedlings (called kresek). Kresek on seedlings may sometimes be confused with early rice stem borer damage. To distinguish kresek symptoms from stem borer damage, Kresek should show yellowish bacterial ooze coming out of the cut ends when leaves squeezed. Unlike plants infested with stem borer, rice plants with kresek are not easily pulled out from soil. On mature plants, lesions usually develop as water-soaked orange stripes on leaf blades or leaf tips. Lesions have a wavy margin and progress toward the leaf base
bacterial_leaf_blight_info_symptoms: Brown, circular to oval spots appear on the coleoptile, which can cause seedling blight and weak, sparse plant stands. Spots are smaller on young leaves and larger on older leaves, ranging from small dark brown or reddish-brown spots to larger oval spots with a dark brown margin and a light reddish-brown or gray center. Similar spots appear on the leaf sheath and hulls. Infected glumes show a general black discoloration, and infected immature florets can produce light-weight or chalky grains.
bacterial_leaf_blight_info_conditions: It can occur in both in irrigated and rainfed lowland areas. Favors temperatures at 25−34°C. It is commonly observed when strong winds and continuous heavy rains occur High humidity Excessive application of nitrogen fertilizer
bacterial_leaf_blight_info_management_se: Application of urea in recommended dosages or application of urea based on leaf colour chart. Ensure good drainage of fields. Immediately after the disease is observed, stop water supply, and let the field dry. When total removal of water is, not possible, try to out-flow water through drainage ditches or water courses (wakkada). Water drained from the fields infected with disease should not be diverted through disease free fields as much as possible. Once the disease is observed, application of potassium fertilizer could manage further spread of the disease.
bacterial_leaf_blight_info_management_ne: Improve soil quality by applying organic fertilizer.
